text:
READ-ONLY BUFFER ANALYSIS — no code changes/builds/tests; current root main includes enum dispatch.

Relevant paths: main.cpp538 a/l vector declarations;564-567 changed-size release;574-586 capacity budget;615-624 resize/zero then timed read wrapper;invoke341-363 full Copy/clear;final821-823 release before stop. Default first program node Copy is already used to skip clearing reused L, but first vector.resize still zero-initializes A and L.

Actual workload arithmetic (from spec, not execution timing): adjacent-size reuse produces9 matrix-pair allocations totaling101,449,728 bytes =96.75MiB of app-level zero stores. A alone and L alone each48.375MiB. Same-size repeated cases already avoid these zeros. Root round2 baseline sum compute median282.35ms vs prep20.73ms and execute215.18ms; remaining~46ms contains allocation/input scan/output/cleanup, NOT pure memset. Old69.9ms allocation profile predates reuse and must NOT justify a69ms gain claim. Likely bandwidth-only savings low single-digit ms; significant fault costs remain legitimately timed. Cannot promise large speedup without A/B.

RECOMMENDED MINIMAL FIRST CANDIDATE: L-only no-init owned array. Replace L vector with a tiny MatrixBuffer RAII wrapper backed by unique_ptr<double[]> allocated using new double[n] (NOT make_unique<double[]>(n), which value-initializes). Give only data/begin/end/size/capacity/empty/reset needed bymain. Could use wrapper for both but initially keep A vector normal. Capacity exactly allocated n, same-size reuse unchanged, changed-size reset before fresh budget as today. For every new/reused L, when the first semantic program node is exactly full Copy, no app clearing; copy overwrites every element, faults happen inside timed kernel/pre-stage Copy. Otherwise fill entire L with0 in the timed region, preserving existing scalar/non-Copy semantics. Official ABI still gets same row-major double* and n/b, no kernel change. Final reset before score stop; fallback before numeric work retains unwritten L until Copy or initialization.

WHY L-ONLY FIRST: requires no special first-touch bookkeeping. The required copy is already timed, so L first-touch remains counted automatically. It eliminates up to48.375MiB redundant application writes in this batch, not allocation fault/OS-zero costs. Small coherent patch, no runtime/core/Metadata edits. Empty program/no-Copy paths stillzero. Never omit a source-level later Copy or clear.

OPTIONAL A FOLLOW-UP: no-init A is legal only if all its pages are WRITE-prefaulted OUTSIDE the IOTime read scope. Otherwise file read absorbs page allocation/fault cost into excludedI/O and falsely improves score, contraryR21. Generic approach: after allocation, in timed region use a volatile unsigned-char pointer, store onebyte at offsets0,page_size,2*page_size,... and last byte (last-byte store covers partial trailing page when allocation isn't page aligned). Page size from sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE) once within score timer; if unavailable, fallback timed fullzero. Volatile ensures sparse stores aren't removed/rewritten as memset. Underlying double objects live from new[], full read overwrites allbytes before finite scan/use. On same-size reuse no new pages need pre-touch. Numeric precision unaffected. But this still pays kernel demand-zero costs, may just trade dense writes for sparse stores, and is extra code/timing subtlety; defer unless L-only wins or measured allocation remains important. No hardcoded4096.

MEMORY/ERROR DETAILS: check elements*sizeof(double) through existing bounds; wrapper count updates only after successful allocation; old pointer released before changed-size fresh allocation so no dual matrix capacity peak. A/l actual capacities feed existing ledger; new[] overhead uses existing allocator slack, not change budget promises. Do not catch late kernel errors to replay. Moving std::copy/fill pointer args leaves semantic stages same. Avoid vector no-init customallocator (unnecessary general allocator complexity) and mmap MAP_POPULATE (new platform policy/cost risk).

MINIMAL VALIDATION WHEN SLOT GRANTED: public20 supplied+strict; R27 functional; repeated-size then smaller/larger mix; synthetic no-Copy scalar reads from initial L expectszero; first Copy underempty/no-op loop relation not falsely recognized; resource fallback; original protocol. Verify score start/IOTime boundaries by source and unchanged per-case mode. Count all allocation, sparse pre-touch (if used), copy, initialization and final free. A/B one candidate at a time, no per-task measurement overhead.

DECISION: L-only is the cleanest small candidate before22:15; main-only wrapper plus simple initialization branch. A-prefault possible but must not be implemented without explicit accounting review. If L-only benchmark is within noise, stop and retain baseline—no structural rewrite justified.

IMPLEMENTED AND CORRECTNESS-VALIDATED: separate round2/buffer worktree from9690887, not dispatch enum branch. Only main.cpp,32added/6removed. OutputBuffer has unique_ptr<double[]> + exact allocated element count; allocate uses new double[elements] (no value init), size/capacity=count; reset clears ownership/count. A stays normal vector with timed value-init. First semantic Copy suppresses L full clear onfresh/reused; any other firstnode/empty program explicitly timed std::fill. Changed-size old buffersreset before budget; adjacent same-size reuse uses capacity count; final free before scorestop. Official calls receive exact original row-major pointer/index/stride. No code inside I/O timer changed. No per-task overhead/Metadata bytes added.

Temporary validation completed and cleaned: clean Releasebuild; public20 serial/parallel eachpublic+strict20/20; existingR27 verify-algorithms allthreePASS; repeated sizes3/90/90/9/120/120 under16MiB total withauto/1MiBgraph cap x atomic/owner numericPASS and expectedresourcefallback flags; no-Copy scalarL+=A shows zeroinitial L onfresh/reused/shrinking/growing matrices forserial/parallel,audit0/1; empty program outputsallzero includingreusedshape. Metadata141B. No formal speedmeasurement.

Analysis only; no builds, tests, benchmarks or production edits yet. Base9690887.

Source findings: main.cpp validate_task performs repeated full string comparisons, workspace callback compares trsm/scalar_expression for every task, work_units loop compares names again, kernel invokes workspace again then invoke does up to6 string checks. Program.operators is already validated against the application's exact allowed public symbols at main initialization; every instantiated call originates from that operator table, while copy/zero are runtime-generated semantic nodes. Existing P007 evidence: 40,722 numerical calls across public20,~283ms total. Added OperatorKind via known-symbol leading byte AFTER exact application allowlist; validate/workspace/work estimate use enum; invoke now enum switch. Kernel classifies once then uses kind for scratch and actual invocation; serial streamer shares one classification for validation+invocation. Parallel preparation separately classifies (cheap) and numerical call once (cheap), no per-Task storage. b^3 loop-invariant moved outside task scan. Unknown symbol still rejected upfront before case allocations/numerics. Copy/zero fixed internal symbols. Need compile slot.

name: round2-page-analysis.txt
scope: development analysis, not scored performance or permanent test suite
text:
READ-ONLY THP FEASIBILITY — 2026-10-30 22:01 CST. No edits/allocations/kernel tests/builds.

ACTUAL HOST: Linux6.6.114.1 WSL2 x86_64; base page4096B. /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled = always [madvise] never; defrag = always defer defer+madvise [madvise] never; hpage_pmd_size2097152B; /proc/self/status THP_enabled1. AnonHugePages0, khugepaged pages_collapsed0/full_scans0 at inspection. Thus MADV_HUGEPAGE is available by policy, but no evidence yet our buffers have ever received THP; only an allocation/inspection experiment can show that. HugePages_Total0 is explicit hugetlb pool, not evidence THP unavailable. Never change system settings/privileges for experiment.

WHY PLAUSIBLE: n1536 double row stride=12288B=3basepages; L total18,874,368B=18MiB=9PMD pages if suitably aligned. b256 kernel row segments are2048B, spread over~3MiB of the same L buffer; the traversal repeatedly touches rows with different4KiB pages. b128 similarly spans~1.5MiB. A is only read/copy source after input; the public numeric kernels operate on L, so L-only advice targets kernel translation behavior without touching file-input timing. No lda/n/b or kernel change required. TLB-benefit claim remains hypothesis; no PMU evidence or timing collected.

PRIMARY DOC CHECK: Linux kernel official transhuge guide https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/mm/transhuge.html. It recommends MADV_HUGEPAGE on critical anonymous mappings, hpage_pmd_size discovery, and warns madvise defrag can invoke synchronous direct reclaim/compaction. THP has transparent basepage fallback. PMD/base sizes vary byarchitecture; do NOT assume2MiB/4KiB on Kunpeng. No MADV_COLLAPSE: newer support, synchronous forcing and differentpolicy semantics would add deadline/risk.

MINIMAL CANDIDATE (requires root approval): independent main.cpp-only OutputBuffer variant from322acfd. At initial config inside scoring, discover basepage and hpage_pmd_size plus policy; if absent/never/incoherent use currentnew[] path unchanged. For sufficiently large L (bytes>=discoveredPMD), request PMD-aligned storage and advise only the fullyowned page-aligned interval before first write. Existing first timedCopy or explicit timedzero triggers actual faults. No reads/writes/prefaults inside excluded inputI/O added. Allocation/alignment/advice/fault/free allwithin existing score timer. Advice failure falls back to normal pages without failing or changing correctness. Do not add diagnostic stat parsing in production hot path; test-only smaps may verify AnonHugePages.

OWNERSHIP/BUDGET: request size rounded UP tobasepage only if actual padded allocationcapacity is charged, and never madvise outside owned interval. AtPMD alignment, n1536 size already exactly9PMD, no padding needed. posix_memalign(alignment,rounded_bytes) with free deleter can own pagealigned memory; watch C++ lifetime/allocator contract and failure code. Conservative reservation must include rounded userbytes plus alignment overhead (up toPMD) because underlyingmalloc may overallocate; check totalcase budget before opting in, otherwise ordinary L allocation fallback. Alternative aligned C++17 new[] can preserve double object lifetime, but exact matched aligned delete/new[] ownership must be correct. Avoid changing Task/core/runtime. Smallbuffers remain oldpath; threshold derives pagegeometry notcaseidentities. No hugepage guarantee and nofixedhardwareconstants.

RISKS: THP madvise defrag may stall on fragmentation; memory footprint/compaction can dominate shortinstances. Aligned malloc may touch tiny bookkeeping pieces insidefirsthuge region and prevent immediatePMD fault unless backed byclean anonymousVMA; actualsmaps verification needed. A64 basepage64KiB => PMD could512MiB, so18MiBLbuffer getsnoPMD andfallback; adaptivebehavior essential. Largerpage alignment can altercache placement while notchangingrowstride; benchmark benefit could be alignment rather thanTHP, so compare alignment-only againstalignment+advice ifpossible.

SMALL TEST: after rootslot, allocate n1536L, advise, execute normaltimedcopy, inspect test-only /proc/self/smaps foraddress andAnonHugePages (verification outside scoredrun; do not claim otherwise). If no THP actual backing, no basis to expecttranslationgain. Then public20+R27 and same/freshsize/resourcefallback checks; A/B rootexclusive withsameCPU/library, fulltime. Testnormalpage fallback via disabled/unavailable advisory branch. Stop if unsupported, costlyorwithinnoise.

Recommendation: policyavailable andtargetedLworking-set structuremakeit a reasonable small lastcandidatebefore22:15, but only ifalignmentreserveandactualpagebackingcan becheckedwithoutwideallocationrewrite. L-only noinit still independent and simpler; do notreplaceacceptedpathwithoutfullA/B.

name: round2-prep-next.txt
scope: development analysis, not scored performance or permanent test suite
text:
READ-ONLY FOLLOW-UP COMPLETE. No source edits/builds/tests.

Recommendation: STOP additional preparation changes in this sleep-before-delivery window; prioritize the root buffer workflow. I do not see a new low-risk metadata-only patch with materially better expected full-time payoff than the now noise-level per-call CSE.

Evidence (existing 3-sample screening, not new measurement):
- baseline full median272.749938ms; summed prepare median19.485277ms (7.14% of full time).
- prepare candidate full271.242545ms; summed prepare19.270144ms (0.215ms lower total prep, noise).
- n1536/b32 baseline prepare9.646743ms; CSE10.441537ms. This does not identify which stage changed, but no robust assembly win.
- n1536/b48 baseline prepare2.126642ms; CSE1.862317ms. Absolute savings small.
- dispatch and combined full272.105/272.455ms with summed prep19.095/19.594ms.
Even deleting ALL preparation is bounded at ~19.5ms /7%, and actually possible changes address only part of it. Do not promise a several-fold win from smaller descriptions.

Why not compact after graph?
Current Task owns symbol + args + reads + writes. Runtime and application kernel path use symbol/args; graph audit uses reads/writes. Clearing read/write vectors after graph would shrink retained heap (largest graph report11.14MB) but (1) does not shrink sizeof(Task) or runtime stride, (2) does not remove the allocations/copies already paid during instantiate, (3) just moves destructor/free work earlier within full timing and adds a pass, (4) would remove independent audit data unless conditional after audit. Net benefit currently unproven. Building a separate compact execution vector copies again and adds validation/budget work; symbols/args already hot through direct task ID. Do not implement this as an assumed speed win.

Why not std::move scratch?
BoundNode scratch is reused for each call site. Moving its vectors into output forces rebuilding/reallocating scratch next iteration and does not reduce the per-instance allocation count. It can change lifetime of pointers and defeat existing scratch reuse.

Why not reserve exact task count?
Generic exact counting means another traversal/interpreter phase unless compiler derives counts; Cholesky formula in runtime is forbidden. std::vector growth moves Task vector/string owners (not deep copies), so capacity reservation alone cannot remove3 small allocations per task. Modest likely benefit, not enough evidence to prioritize.

If time later permits ONE structural candidate, use an allocation arena from the start, not post-graph compaction: Task becomes view/ID descriptor, variable-width arguments/access arrays stored in contiguous storage owned by a TaskBatch/Graph. Keep scratch callback path for serial. This needs coordinated core/metadata/graph/runtime/main/API and budget changes, not minimal patch. It attacks actual per-instance allocations and locality; bounded generic spans support arbitrary external calls. Requires temporary old/new task trace+conflict equivalence, lifetimes across vector growth, fallback before numerics, actual peak-memory accounting. Needs isolated phase profiling first; with the entire prepare ceiling19.5ms, cost-benefit currently unattractive versus current buffer/NUMA issues.

No topology-cache proposal: identical q is a workload observation, not universal proof. Proving topology parameter dependence/caching correctly is a larger algorithmic change and cannot address unique largestq48 first construction anyway.

Parent should retain CSE branch for history but exclude unless final interleaved full benchmark resolves benefit. This advice does not imply preparation is globally optimal; just no material low-risk candidate supported now.

name: round2-priority-cost.txt
scope: development analysis, not scored performance or permanent test suite
text:
READ-ONLY PRIORITY COST ANALYSIS — no implementation changes, no numerical kernel execution, no scored measurements.

Conclusion: changing only priority weights from access volume to approximate FLOPs does NOT provide material evidence to retry the rejected priority implementation for the dominant q6 heavy case. It gives a modest ideal improvement on q12 at12–24workers, but none at32/64 under the base model. Recommend stop; not enough whole-score upside to justify another scheduling implementation before bedtime.

Method actually run (tiny Python, <1s observed tool completion):
- Import current compiler/compile.py to compile actual supplied blocked source+catalog.
- Interpret that parameterized program at b=1,n=q (q4/6/8/12/16); enumerate each access as physical element set.
- Build dependencies with generic last-writer/all-readers from actual task read/write sets, not algorithm edge formulas.
- Exclude first copy/last zero common stages exactly as main does for task DAG scheduling.
- q6 produces56calls/105edges, q12 produces364calls/858edges, matching runtime/public graph counts.
- Nonpreemptive homogeneous processor event simulation: all completed-at-same-time tasks release successors before assigning next ready tasks. Zero scheduler/communication/memory cost.
- True hypothetical task durations (normalized b³/3 units): chol1,trsm3,madd6. A single shape's common b³ factor cancels.
- volume priority uses bottom rank with chol2,trsm3,madd4 from total declared read+write area; FLOP priority uses1/3/6. Source policy picks smallest original task ID; LIFO picks most recently released. These are ideal GLOBAL list policies, not a faithful replay of current per-worker queues/steals/continuation.
- Smaller task ID priority tie by default; reverse tie repeated to check sensitivity. No CPU dispatch latencies, kernel cache effects, task-time variation or heterogeneous local cores are modeled. Results are NOT elapsed milliseconds or predicted target performance.

Base model makespans (smaller better, arbitrary normalized units):

At>=12workers both priority versions already meet intrinsic span51; extra weighting cannot improve this homogeneous ideal. At4/6workers gains1.3%/3.4% versus volume but those are not current full-core target comparisons.

q12: W=1926,S=111.

At24workers FLOP hint improves122→117 =4.10% of ideal q12 execution versus volume; at16workers2.61%; at12workers2.66%. Reverse tie volume at24 gives123 rather than122, FLOP remains117. This is a real modeled difference, but not a material recovery for q6 or full batch. For a ~30ms q12 execution it suggests only ~1.2ms IF model and priority runtime were otherwise free—illustrative scaling only, not predicted measured savings.

Sensitivity (durations altered while comparing same volume vs1/3/6 FLOP rank):
- q6 at12/24/32/64: no difference for duration ratios1:3:6,1:3:9,1:1:2,1:6:12.

Interpretation:
- Priority rankings do differ (55 opposite-order task pairs q6,2818 q12), but most relevant critical work already cannot be delayed with ample processors in ideal model. Inversions alone do not imply makespan improvement.
- Global LIFO can look worse in q12, but prior global priority experiment already attempted to fix that and was slower in actual benchmark. Replacing2:3:4 cost with1:3:6 addresses a smaller secondary effect, not global-lock overhead or locality.
- Official library FLOP ratios are estimates; sqrt/div throughput, b-dependent cache, scratch allocation and memory bandwidth change real durations. Exact application cost hints require measured models on formal library/target or a properly audited complexity contract, not hiding Cholesky DAG formulas.
- Do not redo priority runtime on this evidence. If target traces later show long ready-critical-task delay, root may revisit with actual task-cost calibration; no new permanent timing/audit overhead should be inserted merely to chase this hypothesis.

name: round2-runtime-status.txt
scope: development analysis, not scored performance or permanent test suite
text:
ANALYSIS: root baseline9690887, runtime-only, no compilation/tests started.
Hot-path evidence from code: every numeric task does global completed.fetch_add(acq_rel); every steal does global steals.fetch_add(relaxed). completed/steals/wake_sequence/failed are adjacent fields, so per-task completion/steal writes invalidate lines read by all workers and mix unrelated wake/failure state. Task counts peak19600 on public case; remaining[] notifications still necessary. Historical execute_seconds for tiny kernels can be sub-millisecond to few ms; upper-bound improvement limited to synchronization/dispatch fraction, no claim of speedup or whole-score multiple.
Proposed minimal candidate: batch per-worker completed counts in a local scalar, publish after32 completions OR before any idle transition. A worker must publish before yield/wait, and on normal exit. Last publish reaching n sends final notification. Keep global completion check and acq_rel atomic on each publication. Local steals accumulated and merged once per worker at normal exit. Isolate global completed, steals, wake_sequence, failed on alignas(64) fields to avoid unrelated false sharing (small fixed memory within existing executor slack; no per-task padding/audit). No queue topology or algorithm changes.
Correctness reasoning: published completion sum never exceeds actual finished-task epilogues; equality n can only occur after every task finished. Underpublication can delay stopping but cannot trigger early exit. Every worker with no ready task flushes, so final task chain cannot leave a buffered count sleeping indefinitely. READ-ONLY THP REVIEW — /home/wishapig/hackathon-round2/thp, main.cpp versus322acfd
Reviewed main.cpp SHA256: ab24d933cc6ce3886087aad58e93b7a6ae3a04593e47ad6e6bf63a70ed1bce3f
No repository edits, builds, test executions or scored measurements.

Verdict: no concrete correctness, ownership, scored-timing or budget-subtraction defect found in the current diff (including root-requested ordinary-allocation refund). This is source review, not validation evidence.

Checked paths:
1. OutputBuffer constructor probes THP sysfs once after total_start; aligned allocation, advice and explicit output initialization/copy all occur outside matrix-file IOTime scopes. Ordinary input remains value-initialized before input.read(), so input first-touch does not migrate into excluded I/O. Final output reset is before score stop.
2. Plan only opts in when existing output count==0, THP policy is active/madvise, OS huge-page size is a valid power-of-two multiple of base page, matrix bytes>=huge size, and padding+one full alignment unit is <=available/8. Actual n*n index bounds ensure elements*sizeof(double) cannot overflow on accepted inputs.
3. Allocation uses matching aligned operator new/nothrow and aligned operator delete; success calls uninitialized_default_construct_n for trivial doubles (starts lifetimes without initializing values). On madvise rejection it frees p before ordinary new[]. Reset clears both owners/pointer/count/capacity; no two owners refer to same allocation. No copies or moves of OutputBuffer occur. Trivial double destruction need not be explicitly called before raw deallocation.
4. MADV_HUGEPAGE address is huge-aligned and length is rounded to complete base pages wholly contained in the allocation. It does not advise neighbors/allocator headers; no row-layout/ABI/stride change. THP success is only advice, so it is correct even if OS never promotes pages.
5. Source first-node Copy enables uninitialized output; that whole-copy semantic operation executes before scalar/public numerical work on serial, small-work and executor before-hook paths. If first node is not Copy, full output zero fill occurs before execution. Internal copies are not skipped. Advice does not write/read data.
6. New-shape matrix_bytes accounts ordinary logical L first, then output_plan.extra is deducted before actual allocation. Successful aligned capacity=(padded+huge)/sizeof(double), so actual_extra equals planned extra; ordinary fallback capacity=elements yields actual_extra0 and refunds planned extra. Thus the unsuccessful optimization does not leave a false memory pressure penalty.
7. Same-size reuse: matrix_bytes and retained_matrices include the conservative aligned capacity; plan returns0 because count!=0, so optional extra is not charged twice. Shape change resets l before fresh plan and budget. Allocation attempt never coexists with ordinary fallback because failure advice frees first.
8. Requested total cap remains case_total=min(initial memory budget,fresh headroom+retained accounting); optional THP only subtracts and refunds no more than its reservation. Actual graph budget derives from updated case_budget after refund. Explicit graph cap still takes min; no silent budget override.

Not errors / limits to communicate:
- capacity() means charged allocation reservation, not writable logical element count; begin/end use count, so callers must continue using size for I/O/copy bounds. It includes conservative allocator alignment overhead, not exact RSS. No current caller writes through capacity.
- Alignment reserve may be conservative on platforms where aligned operator new needs less overhead. This can reduce graph allowance slightly, but it is explicit bounded performance tradeoff, not an arithmetic mismatch.
- Runtime global20% headroom remains a snapshot, not a proof against concurrent processes; THP residency is not guaranteed. Target validation/performance needed.
- Class currently cannot be copied because unique_ptr blocks copy; no move emitted because user destructor. Safe current usage is one stable object. Future moves would need custom raw-pointer ownership transfer, but no such call exists here.

Parent should use dispatch-agent actual fallback/advice-rejection/numerical tests and then full benchmark; this review does not claim speedup.

name: round2-wake-analysis.txt
scope: development analysis, not scored performance or permanent test suite
text:
READ-ONLY WAKE ANALYSIS — round2/runtime b5e36a5 (no production edits, builds or tests)

Verdict: gated notifications are possible, but NOT safely by adding `if (sleepers.load()) notify_work()` to the current code. Current producers do not hold wake_mutex; current200us timed wait explicitly masks the predicate-check/unlock race. Removing generation updates or timeout without a handshake can leave ready work parked. A correct smaller-hot-path design needs register-and-rescan plus publisher/waiter wake-mutex coordination. Worth an isolated A/B only if parent has time after first candidates; not a guaranteed improvement.

Observed code, not measured cost:
- push() src/runtime.cpp237-254: every ready enqueue does shared wake_sequence.fetch_add(release) and notify_one, even when all workers active. continuation avoids some pushes already.
- send()295-309: every remote owner event similarly RMW+notify_all; root keeps atomic default, so default gains bounded by ready publishes, not every graph edge.
- work()374 reads wake_sequence every round; parking458-465 relies on200us timeout because publishers do not synchronize with wake_mutex.
- provided graph largest19600 numeric tasks. Ready publications O(V); many continuation tasks have none. Thus max removable work is modest relative to ~70ms heavy56-task case. Avoid promising speedup from V alone.

Minimal race-safe protocol proposal (about three helpers, runtime-only, no API/metadata):
1. Add cache-separated atomic<unsigned> sleepers{0}. Use sequentially-consistent registration/load for a simple proof. Keep a uint64 wake_generation protected by wake_mutex (or keep existing atomic but no hot per-iteration reads).
2. Worker only parks after existing unsuccessful-search/backoff policy. Before parking it flushes its pending completion count. Acquire wake_mutex, increment sleepers, snapshot generation, then recheck terminal predicates AND all possible consumable queues. Atomic backend checks all ready queues under each queue mutex; owner backend also checks its OWN inbox. It must not execute kernel/poll/decrement while wake_mutex held. If a queue is nonempty, unregister, unlock and resume normal work search. Otherwise call cv.wait(lock, predicate generation_changed || failed || completed==n). After wait, decrement sleepers while holding wake_mutex then resume search. Registration must be unwound on exceptions.
3. Producer still enqueues under q.mutex, then RELEASES q.mutex. After publication, read sleepers seq_cst. If zero, return with no wake_generation RMW/notify. If nonzero, acquire wake_mutex, increment generation, release mutex, notify_one for generic ready work. For owner inbox, notify_all so correct owner wakes. Reading sleepers0 is only an optimization; existing OS affinity etc unchanged.
4. Last-completion, failure and shutdown paths always acquire wake_mutex around their generation/terminal notification and notify_all, regardless of sleepers. These rare terminal paths should not use the hot0-sleeper shortcut; this avoids needing a second proof around completed/failed loads. publish_completed remains noexcept: a std::mutex lock may throw! If using mutex inside the RAII noexcept flush, must move terminal wake outside guard or redesign its exception handling rather than introducing terminate(). This is a concrete integration issue with the just-finished batching candidate.
5. Avoid lock inversion: producer must never hold a ready/inbox mutex while acquiring wake_mutex; poll releases inbox before decrement/push, as current code does. Worker may take wake_mutex then queue locks for scan only. No callbacks or failure() calls while holding wake_mutex. No timers are needed for progress once protocol is proved; existing timed wait may remain as defensive backup but cannot be the correctness reason.

Proof sketch for ordinary ready publication:
Let R be sleeper registration; S be its final queue scan; P be producer queue insertion+unlock; L be producer sleeper load. Worker order R->S->wait; producer order P->L->optional wake-mutex update.
- If S sees queued work, worker does not sleep. It need not own it; another worker may steal it, which is still progress.
- If S misses P because S got that queue lock first, queue mutex HB gives R before L. With SC sleeper registration/load and outstanding registration, L cannot see0 (count includes this worker). Producer then needs wake_mutex, which worker holds until cv.wait atomically releases+parks; generation update and notify cannot fall into predicate/wait gap.
- If L sees0 before R, P must precede the later queue scan or its actual work has already been consumed. Either S sees work or someone is making progress. It cannot be simultaneously S-before-P and L-before-R under the queue HB+SC ordering.
- Completion/failure holds wake_mutex for rare terminal publication, so worker's final predicate check and cv atomic wait have no lost-wake gap. All-worker completion still waits active-- drain in run().

Owner backend nuance: a remote event only its owner may consume; generic notify_one can awaken wrong thread and strand owner indefinitely if no future events. Retain notify_all for that event type or implement targeted per-worker condition variables (larger change, not recommended now). Worker final rescan must include its owner inbox, not merely ready queues.

Cost tradeoff / recommendation:
- Busy phase: replace contended wake_generation RMW + library notify with one mostly-read SC load; remove wake_generation acquire load per task round. Potentially positive for tiny-task queue churn.
- Narrow/heavy phase: sleepers commonly nonzero; each publish adds wake_mutex locking plus current notify, possibly slower. Extra full queue sweep on each park O(workers) and sleepers registration RMW also cost. Current public large heavy tasks dominate a substantial part of total.
- Correct proof requires more invasive parking protocol than a two-line optimization and conflicts with noexcept completion guard unless separated carefully. I would NOT implement directly into main. Use a disposable candidate only if first candidate showed synchronization bottleneck or root can afford one controlled A/B; otherwise reject for this deadline.
- Lower-risk alternative (not fully designed here): batch ready notification once per completed task epilogue rather than per newly-ready successor, but this still needs wake-mutex/rescan correctness if removing timeout dependence. It may save fewer calls and adds fanout delay; do not conflate with already-tested batch count knob.

Necessary temporary tests if authorized: deterministic producer-at-register/scan/wait barriers proving no missed notification without timed escape; owner-target sleeping case; all sleepers/final completion; notification before registration; multiple producers+sleepers; empty graph; failure during publication; repeated executor runs; no exceptions from noexcept flush. Then root-only end-to-end5paired samples. No source modification or test run was made for this analysis.
